title: The AI Witch Hunt Keeps Getting It Wrong
author: HobiAI
selftext:
Correct me if I’m wrong, but what I’m seeing is people chasing after real artists they merely suspect of using AI.

At the same time, developers who are honest about using AI — openly tagging it on Steam — aren’t the ones being targeted.

So what exactly is this witch hunt for?
It seems less about ethics or transparency, and more about accusations and guesswork — often aimed at the wrong people.

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body:
Because AI tools remove the direct work and replace it with selecting your favorite out of a large amount of generations. I don't feel like that's a difficult concept. 


Like, people keep going "well if AI isn't art, then neither is Photoshop! Why does digital art get a pass???", but that comparison makes absolutely no sense. Digital art has *never* been remotely as hands off as generative AI - it's always involved direct input and refinable skills, often with a lot of overlap with traditional methods. Especially with modern tools like clip studio paint, krita, whatever, you can adjust what kind of brush you're using, the paint density, the exact shade of color... it's giving you an *extreme* amount of control over the final product, and letting you decide *exactly* how you want the result to look. In every way that matters, the only limit is, in fact, your imagination. 


Meanwhile, generative AI is plain and simple you using someone else's imagination. If it's art, it's because the AI has become intelligent and made creative decisions that you decided not to. Digital art tools could be argued to be the current pinnacle of creative control, where generative AI is the ultimate surrender. 


Even if you use image editing software to fine tune the output of a generative AI, you aren't making your own work, you've just turned yourself into a perfectly fine editor. It's never been okay to take someone else's work, edit it in Photoshop, and call it your own completely original work, and if you tried that you'd get run out.


Why is that okay now that the original artist is a computer?


It isn't the main point, but it also doesn't help that most of the output I've seen in UI design specifically is just so painfully generic. If generative AI is a medium of its own, just expressing the users ideas and creativity, why isn't anyone using it to come up with something half as creative as Metaphor, modern Persona, hell, Expedition 33? Where are all the people using this powerful new tool to express their own unique vision, and why are they getting drowned out under floods of bright primary colors, bubble fonts, and other bog standard design decisions? You'd think that if those existed, we wouldn't hear the end of it, this solid proof that generative AI is a powerful tool for creativity instead of an intended replacement for it. 


But instead, crickets.

replies.author: IncorrectAddress
replies.body:
If I create my own artwork programmatically (procedural art) and allow the system to create my artwork for me, is that ok ?

And then if I build a custom LLM with all my artwork, and then have the AI generate artwork from all my artwork that I have created over the years, is that ok ?

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body:
1: Can be. Depends on how involved the human artist behind it was, and the specific techniques that went into production. 


2: No, because whether it's your work or not, you aren't making your own decisions past which one you like best once the LLM is involved. It's the same thing. 


And besides, "is that okay" is an irrelevant question. The question I'm discussing is "is this art", and art has nothing to do with approval and acceptance and everything to do with self expression. 


Generative AI *impedes* self expression, not enables it.

replies.author: IncorrectAddress

In "self expression" artists will use AI and all digital tools where, whenever, and however they want to, being that this is their choice of "self expression", and as you say it has nothing to do with approval or acceptance for it (opposed to your thoughts, as you seem to think you have rights for approval or acceptance for what an artist is allowed to produce and how they are allowed to produce it), artists can choose to impede or enable any level of "self expression" in the creation of art, using old school techniques to new age tools.

replies.author: SproutsJeremy
replies.body:
> Something is slop because it was made quickly and without much regard for the final product.

Yeah this is true but everybody’s definition of slop is different so the label is kind of pointless unless the product is actually controversial to enough people. Like the 5% of people will call iPhones and all popular mainstream music slop but 95% other people love these things. So the word tends to not hit as hard as the 5% would like it to and the word “slop” is attributed to a bunch of elitists who just want to hate on everything in many contexts. 

In the context of AI it’s a mixed bag, in context of a high quality product that had a mass produced AI workflow incorporated into it, most people won’t view it as slop, but if it’s obviously low quality or low effort, most people will view it as slop. 

Then you have the 5% of that high quality product that will see AI and automatically call it slop even though 95% of that fanbase disagree and it has high reviews everywhere you go. 

Point being, everybody’s definition of slop is different so if a product made with AI is genuinely good and only 5% compared to the 95% believe it’s slop, the 5% can’t really act like they get to dictate the conversation or label it as objectively bad. Especially if most people who choose to side with them are informed on the definition of slop, and therefore what they feel should consititute as slop or not.

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body:
Well, you started this off by saying "Your definition of slop is correct but everyone's definition of slop is different" which... doesn't make sense. It sounds like what you're trying to get at is that there's a lot of people who don't care about overall quality, especially if they can get it quickly, which I wouldn't disagree with. 


That doesn't make it not slop, though. 


In the situation you've outlined, 5% of people are right on what slop is and the rest are wrong. Like, I used this example elsewhere, forget if it was on this topic, but if you run a ton of wagyu beef through an impingement oven, just run all that high quality meat through a conveyor belt cooked identically, even if it's still delicious meat, *it's still slop*. A wagyu beef steak made from the beginning with direct care and attention by a chef will be better, because they can adjust on the fly as needed, cater it to the customer's tastes, whatever their experience tells them will make it better.


With mass production techniques, you'll get a more even experience, but that adaptability and individuality is gone. I like Pizza Hut, but I know that when I make pizza from scratch on my own, I'm working on developing a recipe that's the best for me and my family, and I can adjust it however I like to what we want and need. When we go to a restaurant, or make a frozen pizza, it's faster and easier and it might even be someone's favorite, but that ability to change it exactly how I need to is gone. Even if I add something, make a special request, whatever, there's still a base element that's essentially fixed that can only be changed if I did as much as possible on my own in the first place. 


With food, it's understandable that you're average person just wants to eat something that tastes good, and no one is really too broken up about that. A masterful chef is still going to be able to find work and exercise their craft... but they'll be feeling easy less fulfilled and more stifled if you put them at the end of the Wagyu Cooker and tell them that their job is to season and garnish the mass-produced Wagyu steak now. The more you decide that the artistry isn't worth the time or effort, the more those skills - on both an individual and cultural level - start to degrade and fade from memory. That master chef may still be able to go home and make their steak the way they want, but they're getting way more time making it the fast, cheap way, where before they were spending *all day* honing his craft at the restaurant, and they're not feeling as good about it.


It's the same with art, except where the vast, vast majority of people just eat food for flavor or sustenance, for a whole lot of people who REALLY enjoy media, the analysis and discussion of the story is that interests and excites them, discussing author intent, letting something work it's way into the culture, making its mark with the unique voice of the creator, echoed for each and every piece that's put out, across every skill level on an unrivalled scale.


The art that people make, from a child's drawings to daVinci's paintings, from an amateur love poem to the wild, formula breaking work of E. E. Cummings, *is the culture*, and handing that over to the algorithm to decide what ideas you want to express and how is a sharper blow to the human experience than any Marvel movie or romance novel schlock could ever be. Whatever stage you involved it at, using generative AI is handing over some degree of say over what goes into the final product to a program, in a way that just isn't true for regular digital art, as much as AI boosters will try to argue otherwise. 


There's just no comparison between using digital tools with the same techniques people have been using for thousands of years and telling chatGPT to give you an image, or fill in your line work, or punch up your amateurish scribbles, or make something out of your composition idea. How can someone say that's their original work any more than someone who put some pepperonis on a frozen cheese pizza? How are they any more an artist than that person is a chef? 


The worst part to me is that theb use if generative AI tools like this inherently lowers the bar in a way that cheapens the entire endeavor. It doesn't *democratize* the process the same way that spreading knowledge of good artistic techniques, an eye for quality, or giving people the time and space to practice does, it just tells them that the lowest they should accept AND the highest they can aim for is what the program can put out. Anything below that line becomes unacceptable to them. It IS an actual, existential threat to the appreciation of all forms of art as a human experience, in a way that just doesn't translate to other topics.

replies.author: SproutsJeremy
replies.body:
> Well, you started this off by saying "Your definition of slop is correct but everyone's definition of slop is different" which... doesn't make sense.
    
    I ended up changing my whole comment because double checking it, I didn't really see eye to eye with the way you define slop like I originally thought I did. 
    
    > It sounds like what you're trying to get at is that there's a lot of people who don't care about overall quality, especially if they can get it quickly, which I wouldn't disagree with. That doesn't make it not slop, though. In the situation you've outlined, 5% of people are right on what slop is and the rest are wrong.
    
    Not at all. With things like fast food, mainstream "slop" music, and "slop" shows like Keeping up with the Kardashians, a large portion of the 95% do realize it's slop even if they do enjoy it. So in discussions you find the majority accepting the label. 
    
    We're talking about cases, for example, with mainstream music where the 95% says this is genuinely good music and in no shape or form slop, but the 5% dismiss it as slop just because they believe it is low quality, it was quickly produced, and by their metrics, there was not much care or thought put into it. Artists and companies can ship out many products at a fast pace. That doesn't mean there wasn't years of thought, effort, and care that went into getting them to that point where they are dropping highly valued products at a yearly, monthly, weekly, or even daily basis. I've seen many artists drop genuinely good hand drawn art daily. That doesn't automatically make it slop, but in some cases it can be. Same with AI if you're true to the actual definition of slop, and not your own definition you created to satisfy your own ideology. 
    
    > A wagyu beef steak made from the beginning with direct care and attention by a chef will be better, because they can adjust on the fly as needed, cater it to the customer's tastes, whatever their experience tells them will make it better.
    
    Like I said in my previous comment (the new edit), I know nothing about beef, I eat fish. Sometimes fish coming from the fast food shop will just taste better than a chef at a fancy restaurant. I've had bad tasting fish that was "made from the beginning with direct care and attention by a chef", and so have most of the people I've known. So I don't feel like this is the best argument to use.
    
    > The more you decide that the artistry isn't worth the time or effort, the more those skills - on both an individual and cultural level - start to degrade and fade from memory. 
    
    This is definitely true but people will always find worth in the art regardless of how good AI gets. You and many people who think like you are proof of that and you don't have to bash others or call what they make slop to justify valuing human made work.
